newsitem.title: SWEDEN: BALTICS - CENTRAL BANKERS UNCONCERNED ABOUT C/A DEFICITS.
newsitem.headline: BALTICS - CENTRAL BANKERS UNCONCERNED ABOUT C/A DEFICITS.

text.p: Baltic central bankers said on Thursday that they were not overly concerned about their countries' relatively high current account deficits, which observers say stem partly from their rigid exchange rate systems.

"It (a current account deficit) is a common feature of most economies in transition and is not a negative thing," Einars Repshe, the governor of the Bank of Latvia, told a conference on Baltic capital markets in the Swedish capital.
"Lithuania's current account deficit is within sustainable limits," Lithuanian central bank chief Reinoldijus Sharkinas told the conference.
"In 1995, it was 10.3 percent of Lithuania's gross domestic product (GDP), and in 1996 it was 8.2 percent of GDP," he said.

Estonian deputy central bank governor Peter Lohmus conceded that it could be a problem but said that much of his country's deficit, currently about 10.5 percent of GDP, was attributable to capital goods and investment.
All three rejected the idea of devaluing their currencies to rectify the situation, saying instead that local companies needed to become more competitive.
Lithuania and Estonia both peg their currencies rigidly under a currency board system, while the Latvian lat is tied to the IMF's SDR.
The rigid pegs have been partly blamed by some for the region's current account deficits.
In Lithuania, the prime minister and other senior government officials have warned that the country could face a Mexican-style crisis down the road as a result.
"The currency board does not provide for changes in the exchange rate," said Lithuania's Sharkinas.
"Instead, enterprises must become competitive," he said.
Exports rose in Lithuania last year by over 20 percent, the highest growth in Eastern Europe.
Lohmus said that Estonian companies had responded by becoming more competitive and that the country's exports were rising.
